responses.title: How the IR Turret Listens and Acts
story: Picture the turret as a sleepy guard sitting by a door, waiting for a knock. At the start, it wakes up, plugs in its three motors, turns on its remote-control eye, and walks to its home pose. Then it does one thing forever: listen.

When you press a button, the remote blinks an invisible light made of tiny flashes. The eye reads the flashes and turns them into a number called a command code. The turret then checks that number against its list of buttons.

If the number matches, it runs the move you asked for. Arrows turn and tilt it, OK fires one dart, star fires all six, 1 nods yes, and 2 shakes no. Then it goes back to listening, ready for the next press.

steps.label: Name the buttons
steps.detail: Each remote button gets a nickname for its secret number, like left meaning 0x8, so the code is easy to read.

steps.label: Set up motors
steps.detail: The three servos (the turret's motors) are named, and settings like turn speed and dart timing are stored in variables.

steps.label: Wake up
steps.detail: The setup function runs once: it plugs the servos into pins 10, 11 and 12, starts the IR eye on pin 9, and moves to home.

steps.label: Catch a signal
steps.detail: The loop keeps asking if the eye caught a signal, then calls resume so it can hear the next button.

steps.label: Pick the action
steps.detail: The switch looks at the command number and jumps to the matching button, such as up, OK or star.

steps.label: Do the move
steps.detail: Turning works by spinning the yaw motor for a short time and then stopping it. Firing spins the roll motor for one sixth of a turn per dart.

responses.metaphor: The turret is like a guard with a list of secret knocks, and each knock on the remote tells it which trick to do.
responses.watch_for: Press OK and the barrel should spin a little for one dart, then press star and it should spin a full turn to fire all six.
